note: One entry per rule whose positive case could plausibly also be a TypeScript error. `scripts/tsc-oracle-gate.mjs` compiles each `code` against the real published typings (fixtures/tsc-oracle/packages.json) and enforces `expect`. See docs/precision-backlog.md for the full redundancy ledger, of which this file is the executable part.

expectations.silent: TypeScript must report nothing. The rule's claim is therefore its own. A diagnostic here means the rule now duplicates `tsc` and must be narrowed or deleted -- that is the gate AGENTS.md's absolute rule was missing.
expectations.distinct-claim: TypeScript does report something, but about a different defect than the finding asserts. Requires `allow` (the diagnostic codes seen) and `why` (what the finding claims that the type error does not). Never use this to keep a rule whose claim is the type error's claim.
expectations.removed-because-redundant: TypeScript must report a diagnostic. The rule that used to fire here was deleted for exactly that reason, and this direction is pinned so that a future Solid release which loosens the type -- making `tsc` silent again -- fails this gate and forces the removal to be reconsidered rather than quietly leaving a hole.

cases.why: SC3004, removed 2026-08-17. `EffectFunction` returns `(() => void) | void`, so every spelling the rule proved -- contextual, explicit, returned call, member -- is a type error. `(() => void) | void` is a union, not bare `void`, so return-value-ignoring assignability does not rescue it.

The legal spellings the removed rule accepted. Pinned so the removal cannot be re-justified by a type that rejects *everything*: the type draws the same line the rule drew, which is what made the rule redundant rather than merely weaker.

SC9002, removed 2026-08-17. The obligation's whole domain was the *legality* of a returned value, and the type system closes legality: a mixed union and an `unknown` return are type errors, and the second argument being a non-callback value at all is a type error.

The rest of SC9002's domain, and the reason narrowing it was not an option. `any` leaves `tsc` silent, but `any` is missing evidence rather than proof of a defect (AGENTS.md). The `{ effect, error }` bundle is a supported API form -- `EffectBundle` -- so the obligation the rule raised there was noise on idiomatic code, not a limit worth reporting.

SC7003, removed 2026-08-17. `Refreshable<T> = T & { readonly [$REFRESH]: any }` encodes the source brand *as a type*, so every target shape the rule proved invalid -- a wrapper thunk, a read value, an object literal, a plain accessor, a store child record, and a value-form store -- is TS2345 against it. A valid target type-checks, so the type draws the same line the rule drew.

The valid targets, pinned so the removal cannot be justified by a type that rejects everything. `refresh(memo)` and `refresh(signalGet)` type-check because `createMemo`/`createSignal` return `Refreshable` accessors.

SC7004, removed 2026-08-17. A key on an accessor target selects the one-argument `affects(target: Accessor<unknown> | Store<object>)` overload, whose second parameter does not exist, so TypeScript reports TS2345 on the key itself -- exactly the rule's claim.
The legal `affects` forms from the rc.0 doc comment: a bare accessor, a store record, and a record plus one of its own keys.

SC9003, both names, removed 2026-08-17. The obligation asked whether the target carries the source brand, and the brand is a type: an untraceable target is TS2345 and a branded one type-checks, so there was nothing left to be uncertain about.

SC7001 is independent. The single-argument `createEffect(compute)` overload still exists in rc.0 -- deprecated, and typed to return `never` -- so `tsc` accepts the call. The finding's claim is that the effect never runs, which no part of that signature says.

SC4004 is independent, and it is the consumer that kept the cleanup-return *classification* alive after SC3004 went. Returning a real cleanup from an unowned `onSettled` is perfectly typed; the claim is that nothing will ever dispose it -- an ownership fact.
SC4002 is independent. `onCleanup` takes a `Disposable` and this argument is one; the claim is that no owner is active at the call, which is a runtime ownership fact.
cases.code:
import { onCleanup } from "solid-js";
onCleanup(() => {});

cases.why: SC1002 is independent. Reading an accessor after an `await` is type-correct in every respect; the claim is about when the read happens relative to the tracking scope.

SC8007 is independent, and this is the case that shows the JSX family is not uniformly redundant: `EventHandlerUnion` includes `BoundEventHandler`, so the `[handler, data]` tuple is *legal* per Solid's own types. The claim is that the bound form defeats handler identity comparison, which no type expresses.
cases.code:
const handler = (data: number, event: MouseEvent) => {};
export const Case = () => <button onClick={[handler, 1]} />;

Two *differently spelled* props that the compiler lowers into one slot -- `onClick`/`onclick` both become the delegated `el.$$click` write -- are distinct, legal properties to TypeScript. Its byte-identical-name domain is TS17001 and is recorded as redundant in docs/precision-backlog.md.

cases.why: SC8001's unknown-`on*`-name arm, audited 2026-08-17 and recorded redundant in docs/precision-backlog.md (narrowing not yet landed). An unknown name does not exist on the element's attribute type, and Solid 1.x's only JSX index signature is `[key: `-${string}`]`, so nothing absorbs it. The rule SURVIVES on its declared-spelling arms -- see the sibling `silent` case.
cases.code: export const Unknown = () => <div onFoo="a" />;

cases.why: SC8011's intrinsic-element arm, audited 2026-08-17 and recorded redundant in docs/precision-backlog.md (narrowing not yet landed). Each React spelling is individually absent from the element's attribute type. The rule SURVIVES on components whose props admit the key -- see the sibling `silent` case.
cases.code: export const Case = () => <label className="field" />;

cases.why: SC8017's object-key arms, audited 2026-08-17 and recorded redundant in docs/precision-backlog.md (narrowing not yet landed). Both are covered by `csstype`: a camelCase key is TS2561 with the kebab-case suggestion, and a unitless number for a length is TS2322. The rule SURVIVES on every string-valued `style` -- see the sibling `silent` case.
cases.code: export const Camel = () => <div style={{ maxWidth: 3 }} />;

cases.why: SC8001's surviving arms, and the reason the rule was not deleted. `onclick` and `ondblclick` are *declared* props in Solid 1.x, so TypeScript accepts them and the canonical-casing advice is the rule's own. A spread-carried handler type checks while Solid does not attach it. And a hyphenated tag is TS2339 against stock typings, so a project using one has declared it -- the augmentation here is the permissive shape such declarations commonly take -- after which TypeScript is silent about its attributes and the static-value and ambiguous-name arms are the only claims available.

SC8011's surviving arm, and upstream's own cases 4, 8 and 9. A component's props are whatever it declares, so a React spelling on a permissive component is an ordinary permitted key and `tsc` is silent.

SC8017's surviving arms. A string `style` is legal in Solid 1.x, so the string-value advice, the malformed-declaration claim, and the not-CSS-at-all claim are all the rule's own; a `-`-prefixed key is absorbed by the `[key: `-${string}`]` index signature.
